title: Krishna Becomes Every Calf and Boy
story:
One day the calves and the cowherd boys of Vrindavan — the little forest village where Krishna was growing up — vanished, and no one could say where they had gone. The boys had walked out that morning with their staffs and their flutes, driving the calves before them, and they simply did not come back. As the afternoon stretched toward evening, mothers stood in their doorways, listening. The cows shifted in their pens and lowed into the quiet for calves that did not answer. The whole village seemed to have lost its young at once.

Krishna had been with the boys, and he alone knew what had become of them. He could have set every child and every calf back in his own place with a word. But he chose a gentler way, one meant not merely to repair what was missing but to give something to the mothers and the cows who were waiting. He became them. Standing at the edge of the pasture, Krishna stretched himself into every vanished calf and every vanished boy, taking on not only each face and pair of limbs but everything that made that child that particular child — his staff and his horn, his flute and the leaf in his hand, his ornaments and his clothes, and deeper than these, his temper, his way of talking, his name, his age, the very way he walked and played. The old verses say that every one of those boys and calves was Krishna himself, whole and complete.

Then each boy gathered his own calf and walked home to his own house. In the cow-pens the cows hurried forward, calling to their calves with a lowing that filled the evening air, and the calves ran to them as though they had never been away. In the houses, mothers rose at the first note of a flute, ran out, and lifted their sons into their arms. They held them close and would not put them down — kissing them, washing them, dressing them, marking their foreheads with tilak, the red mark of blessing, and setting food before them. They asked nothing, and needed no answer. The lost thing had come back, and that was all they wanted.

And the strange, tender part was this: the love did not simply return. It grew. The cows loved their calves, and the women loved their sons, with a warmth greater than they had felt before — because what they held in their arms was Krishna himself, wearing a different child's face, and not one of them suspected it.

So it went for a full year. Morning after morning the boys who were Krishna drove the calves who were Krishna out to the pastures, and evening after evening they came home to mothers who were loving Krishna without knowing it. The affection in those homes climbed the way a vine climbs, leaf by leaf, in a season no one counts. And no one ever guessed — not the mothers, not the cows, not even the boys themselves. All year long the village kissed its children goodnight, and every small forehead under those kisses was Krishna's.
reflection: The episode turns on a quiet paradox: the mothers' love deepened precisely when its object was Krishna, though they did not know it. Love, the story suggests, is not made less real for being offered in ignorance — it is simply received by the one who was always its true object.
next_story_tease: Yet a wildfire was soon to sweep through the forest toward the herd.
hero_scene: In the doorway of a cowherd home a mother lifts her small son high and kisses his head, while in home after home across Vrindavan other mothers do the same with their own boys — every one of them Krishna, wearing a different child's face.
visual_elements: Krishna in a hundred borrowed boy-forms
